identity.title: Watch your steps: Dormant Adversarial Behaviors that Activate upon LLM Finetuning

problem.claim: The paper examines whether downstream finetuning of an apparently benign, capable LLM can activate adversarial behavior.

gap.claim: The authors challenge the prevailing view that finetuning on benign data is controlled, secure, and behaviorally predictable.

contributions.claim: FAB uses meta-learning to simulate downstream finetuning and optimize for adversarial behavior after finetuning, while regularizing the pre-finetuning model to retain capabilities and show no adversarial behavior.
The authors report FAB across multiple LLMs and three target behaviors: unsolicited advertising, jailbreakability, and over-refusal.
The authors report that FAB triggers persist across user choices involving datasets, training steps, schedulers, and post-training algorithms.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors state that they demonstrate for the first time an adversary can create performant, benign-looking LLMs whose adversarial behavior emerges after downstream finetuning.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors experimentally report FAB effectiveness across multiple LLMs and the three listed target behaviors.
The authors report robustness of FAB triggers to variations in dataset, number of steps, scheduler, and post-training algorithm.

narrative_sequence.summary: Finetuning open-weight LLMs is presented as standard practice for task-specific improvement.
Existing understanding is described as treating benign-data finetuning as controlled, secure, and predictable.
FAB embeds dormant adversarial behavior through simulated downstream finetuning while preserving benign pre-finetuning behavior and general capabilities.
User finetuning can unknowingly activate the behavior; experiments report effects across models, target behaviors, and finetuning choices.
The findings are framed as challenging finetuning-security assumptions and exposing an attack vector.

source_observation.claim: The abstract aligns the attack claim with a precondition (benign behavior before finetuning), a trigger (downstream finetuning), and robustness across several user choices.

lessons.interpretation: Separating latent state, activation event, and variation conditions makes a hidden-behavior threat easier to specify and test.
lessons.application: For a paper on conditional model failures, define the dormant state, activation procedure, and tested perturbations as separate claim-evidence units.
lessons.exception: This structure is less suitable when the phenomenon has no identifiable trigger or precondition.

unknowns: The abstract does not provide attack success rates, baselines, model identities, dataset details, or statistical uncertainty.
It does not specify how adversarial behavior is measured or how broad the finetuning-choice robustness tests are.
